newsitem.title: UK: Vulnerable oil price limits OPEC's options.
newsitem.headline: Vulnerable oil price limits OPEC's options.

text.p: A $2 a barrel drop in oil prices in just a week and the lingering prospect of a sudden return of Iraqi crude exports dashes any expectations that OPEC may have had to increase production, OPEC delegates and analysts say.

When the 11 ministers of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) meet at the end of the month in Vienna, they are virtually certain to hold the output ceiling unchanged at 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd) for the first half of 1997, they say.
"It looks certain that we will maintain the status quo. It may have been different if the prices were much higher or much lower than what we have now," an OPEC official said.
This official said the meeting could end shortly after it begins on November 27 since there is so little for the ministers to discuss.
"Short and sweet, that is what we are predicting. It will yet again be a case of wait and see on Iraq," the official said.
A blistering and prolonged rally has taken the price of oil beyond oil producers' wildest dreams and stunned oil analysts who had forecast much lower prices.

Fears that heating oil supplies on both sides of the Atlantic would fall short in the winter and political tensions in the oil-rich Middle East combined to push world benchmark North Sea Brent crude to a post nearly six-year high of $25.06 in mid-October.
However, mild weather and a steady climb in U.S. heating oil inventories since then has encouraged some selling and taken nearly $3 off the price.

OPEC delegates say the relatively high oil price has vindicated OPEC's decision in June to keep mum about quota busting and not cut output to make room for an expected return of Iraqi exports under a United Nations oil-for-food scheme.
In June, OPEC raised its ceiling to 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd) to reflect a rise of 700,000 bpd in Iraqi output expected when the U.N. plan was implemented.
But that plan was put on hold after military confrontation between Baghdad and Washington after Saddam Hussein was involved in Kurdish fighting in northern Iraq in August.
"Ironically it probably would have been better for us to see the Iraqi oil return now when demand is high rather than still have this uncertainty hanging over our heads," a OPEC Gulf delegate said.
Analysts reckon that OPEC coffers will be $20 billion to $25 billion better off because of the windfall.
"OPEC has benefited from the rally. There is no sense in spoiling a good thing," said Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at brokers Smith Barney.
OPEC heavyweight Saudi Arabia and other influential Middle East Gulf producers are also keen to keep quiet about the rampant quota violations of most members.
Most independent observers believe OPEC is producing nearly one million bpd over its own ceiling.

"Since all but three members -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE -- are producing as much as they can, no one is likely to push too hard for any increase," said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist at Swiss bank UBS.
A public OPEC row could stampede jittery futures markets to skim the top off the price if oil traders believe such a spat could fracture the once-mighty cartel.
"Any increase would be a cosmetically bad signal for the market. The OPEC Secretariat itself forecasts an extraordinarily low demand for its own oil next year," UBS' Pyne said.
The latest OPEC Secretariat report predicts demand for OPEC oil in 1997 will average only about 25 million.
That is well below the 26 million the group now pumps out even before the return of some Iraqi oil exports.
